title: The Last Man on Earth

evidence.note: The two Internet Archive items carry different designations. TheLastManOnEarthHD is marked Public Domain Mark 1.0 and TheLastManOnEarth_72 is marked CC0 1.0. Both are uploader labels, not rights determinations. A US work published in 1964 would normally be protected for 95 years, until 2060. Public domain status would therefore depend on a missing copyright notice or a missing renewal. No notice-defect documentation, registration record or renewal search was located in this session, so the print status is not confirmed.
evidence.source: Cornell University Library — Copyright & Fair Use: Public Domain

evidence.note: This is a US–Italian co-production. The Internet Archive metadata credits directors Ubaldo Ragona and Sidney Salkow. The URAA (1994) restored US copyright for foreign works that were still protected in their home country on the restoration date, even if the work had lost US protection through a formality failure. Whether the Italian authorship brings restoration into play depends on the Italian authors' death dates and Italy's term at that time. Neither was verified in this session, so the restoration question is unresolved.
evidence.source: Cornell University Library — Copyright & Fair Use: Public Domain (URAA section)

evidence.note: This is a sound film. The recorded score in the soundtrack normally shares the film print's copyright status, so the score layer follows the unresolved print layer. No separate registration of the score was located.

The Internet Archive metadata states that the film adapts Richard Matheson's novel 'I Am Legend'. Matheson's source work is a separate copyrighted work that is treated as still in force. Under Stewart v. Abend, a derivative work cannot be exploited during the underlying work's copyright term without the owner's permission, so the source story can restrict reuse of the film regardless of the print's status. The novel's registration and renewal records were not pulled in this session.
evidence.source: Stewart v. Abend, 495 U.S. 207 (1990) — Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute

evidence.note: No trademark registration for the title or franchise was checked in this session. The 'I Am Legend' name is used in other commercial adaptations, so avoid franchise naming in titles or branding.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
Modern HD remasters and colorized versions carry new protectable elements.

editorial:
The Last Man on Earth (1964) is a science fiction horror film starring Vincent Price as Dr. Robert Morgan, the sole healthy survivor of a plague that has devastated the planet. It was directed by Ubaldo Ragona and Sidney Salkow, runs about 86 minutes, and adapts Richard Matheson's novel 'I Am Legend'. Two Internet Archive items host it, one in 720p HD and one alternate transfer. Both are labeled as free of restrictions, but the labels differ (Public Domain Mark 1.0 and CC0 1.0).

The rights trap has two parts. First, the print's free status is unconfirmed. A 1964 US publication would normally last until 2060 unless a notice or renewal was missed, and no such record was found. The film's Italian co-production origin also leaves a possible URAA restoration claim open. Second, Matheson's novel is a separate work that is still treated as protected. Under Stewart v. Abend, a new commercial adaptation or reuse of the story can require a license from the source's owner even if the print itself is free.
faq: The film is hosted everywhere as public domain. Is that confirmed?

No. The Internet Archive's Public Domain Mark and CC0 labels are uploader designations. A 1964 US film is protected until 2060 unless it lost protection through a missing notice or renewal, and this research did not locate a record showing either. Its Italian co-production origin also leaves a possible URAA restoration claim unresolved.
Can I make a new adaptation based on this film?

Not without clearing the underlying novel. Richard Matheson's 'I Am Legend' is a separate copyrighted work. Under Stewart v. Abend, its owner can restrict commercial use of a derivative film's story even if the film print is free to use.
